canberra.title: Hanson accuses PM and Treasuer of inciting violence against her
canberra.snippet: Pauline Hanson has accused Anthony Albanese of inciting violence towards her by saying she and her One Nation party are divisive and dang...
canberra.content:
Pauline Hanson campaigning in WA for the Secret Harbour byelection last week. The One Nation leader says the Prime Minister and Treasurer have ‘crossed a line’. Photo: Pauline Hanson.

Pauline Hanson has accused Anthony Albanese of inciting violence towards her by saying she and her One Nation party are divisive and dangerous.

The Prime Minister delivered a strong rebuke of One Nation on Sunday (30 August) when addressing the party faithful at the Queensland State Labor Conference.

The day before, One Nation had snatched a seat from Labor to claim victory in a Western Australian state byelection.

“We have a Liberal Party that isn’t liberal, a National Party that isn’t national, and One Nation, whose leader seeks to divide Australians; talks Australia down both here and overseas,” Mr Albanese told conference delegates.

Later in his speech, the PM went further, describing Australia and the labour movement as at a crucial time.

“Across the world hard right populists are on the march,” he said.

“Peddling politics that is dangerous, divisive, and downright dishonest.

“We simply must defeat them. We owe it to history. And we will defeat them … They’ll say anything and do anything to win votes. Bend any facts. Peddle misinformation and disinformation. Turn Australian against Australian.

“Parties like One Nation have no serious answers to our problems.”

At the same conference, Treasurer Jim Chalmers also described One Nation as a “dangerous threat” to Australia.

“The threat to our country and its cohesion, its people, and our economy is posed by a dangerous and divisive coalition of chaos – a three-ring circus of Liberals, Nationals, and One Nation,” Dr Chalmers said.

“Today the biggest fault lines in our politics aren’t just between the centre-left and the extreme right, but between those of us who want to address and alleviate the legitimate frustrations that people feel about the cost of living and other pressures, and those who just want to picket them and prey on them, to politicise them and capitalise on them, while leaving our major challenges largely undisturbed.”

On Monday, Senator Hanson said the Prime Minister and his Treasurer Jim Chalmers had “crossed a line” in the way they had described her and One Nation.

She said such emotive language can incite political violence, as it did in the United Kingdom with the murder in July of former British conservative MP Ann Widdecombe.

The One Nation leader posted a lengthy social media post to denounce the pair and their speeches.

“The attacks from Chalmers and Albanese on One Nation have become increasingly desperate. Yesterday they crossed a line,” she wrote.

“No matter how worried Jim and Albanese are about losing their jobs, telling Australians that their democratically elected opponents are ‘dangerous’ and a ‘threat to our country’ invites people to treat them as a threat.

“Words have consequences. That is how political violence is incited.

“The murder of Ann Widdecombe in Britain should be warning enough about the dangers of poisonous political rhetoric.

“Anthony Albanese says we need to turn down the heat and violent rhetoric in our political discourse.

“Meanwhile, he and his Treasurer are pouring petrol all over it.”

Senator Hanson said Australians are entitled to vote for One Nation without being told by the Treasurer and the Prime Minister that their democratic choice is a danger to the nation.

“The real danger is that Jim and Albanese’s incompetent economic management will continue to push your rent, your mortgage and your bills even higher,” she said.

“The real danger to Jim and Albanese is that the people of Australia are coming for their government … at the ballot box.”

The One Nation leader subsequently posted that she supported free speech and open debate as “fundamental parts of our democracy”, but drew the line at “normalising and encouraging” potential incitements to violence.

“Jim Chalmers and Anthony Albanese crossed that line yesterday in their attacks on One Nation,” she said.

“Free speech and open debate is only possible when everyone is protected from the threat of violence in response to what they say.

“Labor politicians seem to get a free pass to use language they would never allow others to use.

“When democratically elected parties are described as ‘threats’ and a ‘danger to the country’ by the Prime Minister and the Treasurer, people will take those words seriously.

“Jim Chalmers and Anthony Albanese need to take their own advice and ‘turn the temperature down’.”

One Nation’s win in the WA state electorate of Secret Harbour is the first the party has secured in that state’s Lower House and shows it is not only a threat to the Coalition but also to Labor.

Federal Liberal frontbencher Andrew Hastie holds the seat of Canning, which encompasses the state electorate One Nation has just won.

canberra.title: Drink ‘spiker’ sentenced for role in violent ordeal that left woman with 44 injuries
canberra.snippet: After having her drink ‘spiked’, a woman was trapped in a car and violently assaulted for two hours before she managed to esc...
canberra.content:
Casey-Lee Pricsina, 35, has been sentenced by the ACT Supreme Court. Photo: Michelle Kroll.

After having her drink ‘spiked’, a woman was trapped in a car and violently assaulted for two hours before she managed to escape.

One member of the trio behind the incident, Raymond Kevin Ziebell, was handed six-and-a-half years’ jail over his role last year before it was Casey-Lee Pricsina’s turn to be sentenced by the ACT Supreme Court.

The female victim met Ziebell and Pricsina, who had been in a relationship at the time, through a mutual contact before they went to her home in December 2023 to repair her fence.

Pricsina returned to the woman’s home late the next night and asked to come inside before they shared a drink. The woman left her drink unattended on occasion that evening, and on her return, thought it tasted weird, like medicine.

Ziebell also arrived before Priscina convinced the woman to go with them to a McDonald’s.

They got into Ziebell’s car, and he drove off before the woman realised there was a third person inside the vehicle, the then-35-year-old Kristie Lee Watson of Scullin.

For the next two hours, the trio trapped the woman inside the car, accused her of taking drugs or money and threatened to cut her up and get to her daughter before one, alleged to be Watson, demanded $10,000.

Acting Justice Louise Taylor, in her recently-published decision, said Watson repeatedly punched the woman in the face and also repeatedly hit her in the face with a metal bat, dislodging one of her teeth.

When Ziebell finally pulled over, he threatened to cut the woman up with an electric saw before burying her where they stopped.

He also strangled her until she couldn’t breathe, put his knee in her chest and punched her in the face.

Raymond Kevin Ziebell (left) tries to hide his face from media after leaving court. Photo: Albert McKnight.

The woman managed to get out of the car and started running, but Ziebell and Watson chased her and tripped her up. She again managed to escape and ran to the Molongolo Water Quality Control Centre in Holt, near Shepherds Lookout.

She was taken to hospital with 44 different injuries over her body.

“Since then, my life has narrowed to a corridor of fear and isolation,” the woman went on to tell the court.

“I rarely leave the house and find shopping malls unbearable. At night, I have to lock my daughter and myself in our room to find some sense of safety to fall asleep.”

Pricsina pleaded guilty to recklessly inflicting grievous bodily harm and forcible confinement, both by joint commission.

Acting Justice Taylor said she was jointly criminally liable for everything inside the car until it stopped, when Ziebell and Watson went beyond the agreement they had made with her.

The acting justice said Pricsina hadn’t inflicted the violence herself that night, but she lied to the woman to engender her sympathy and to encourage her trust and also “spiked” her drink in an effort to facilitate the offending.

“This deception was critical to the victim’s eventual willingness to leave the safety of her residence and voluntarily enter the vehicle,” the judge said.

Acting Justice Taylor did say Ziebell had exerted a level of manipulation and control over Pricsina in their relationship, which influenced her in becoming involved in the offences.

Pricsina had a disadvantaged childhood and began using drugs when she was 14. She is now aged 35, is unemployed and said she had received Centrelink payments for about 15 years.

She was sentenced to about three years and one month’s jail with a one-year and five-month non-parole period, which means she can be released from custody in December 2027.

Watson died in August 2025.

canberra.title: Wagga Council issues $110 fine to homeless pensioner at Wilks Park
canberra.snippet: Housing advocates have condemned Wagga Wagga City Council for issuing a $110 fine to a disabled pensioner living in a bus at Wilks Park. ...
canberra.content:
31 August 2026

Start the conversation

A fine Wagga Council issued to a pensioner on Monday. Photos: Supplied.

Housing advocates have condemned Wagga Wagga City Council for issuing a $110 fine to a disabled pensioner living in a bus at Wilks Park.

The man was among at least three people fined by council compliance officers on Monday (31 August) after refusing to leave the park.

Council compliance officers and NSW Police had previously visited Wilks Park on 11 August, issuing dozens of letters telling people they had to vacate the site by Tuesday, August 25, or risk being fined.

Many rough sleepers at the park had been offered what the NSW Government calls “temporary accommodation” – essentially hotels and motels.

But with every hotel room in Wagga booked out on 25 August, council officers did not undertake any compliance action that day.

At least three people were issued fines on Monday, including the disabled pensioner living in the bus.

The fines were issued for failing to comply with the “terms of a notice erected by council”.

Housing advocates noted that the police and compliance officers had been respectful and courteous, but the issuing of penalty notices was distressing for people who had nowhere else to go.

“I really don’t know what they are supposed to do; they don’t have the money to pay the fines,” Tim Verhoef said.

He said moving into a hotel was not the answer because people did not want to give up all their possessions to move into a small room temporarily.

Wagga Council defended its actions in a statement released on Monday.

“Council staff and NSW support agency staff are attending Wilks Park from today as part of a three-day compliance operation to address ongoing breaches of the site’s conditions of stay,” a spokesperson said.

“Throughout the operation, council staff will continue to encourage anyone sleeping or residing in temporary structures at the site to take up the accommodation and support services being offered. Homes NSW and Vinnies have continued to actively engage with people living at Wilks Park and other identified homelessness encampments, offering accommodation and support to assist with relocation.

“Most individuals have actively engaged with support services and accepted accommodation options. Council has provided additional time for people to make arrangements before commencing formal compliance action and has offered temporary storage facilities to assist those transitioning into housing.”

Police and compliance officers at Wilks Park on Monday.

The council said it would not fine people who engaged with support services.

“However, several people staying at Wilks Park have consistently declined offers of accommodation and support. Compliance action will now be undertaken where individuals continue to stay at the site in breach of the conditions of stay.”

Wagga councillor Richard Foley said fines were not the answer.

“It’s a pointless exercise to issue fines to people who don’t have the capacity to pay,” he said.

“But while council are looking like the bogeyman, it’s the NSW Government who are at fault. I offered them a positive solution to this crisis immediately after a baby died in the tent, but they have ignored us.”

In May, Cr Foley sent Housing Minister Rose Jackson a submission outlining a pilot proposal to establish a modular tiny-home village supported by wraparound services to address the homelessness crisis.

He said he had not even received an acknowledgment of his submission.

Wagga Council said it would also continue to clean up former campsites and restore Wilks Park to its intended use for the wider community.

“Wilks Park is a primitive campground that provides basic facilities and permits stays of up to 72 hours,” a spokesperson said.

Kira Levin, principal solicitor of the Homeless Persons’ Legal Service at the Justice and Equity Centre, said anyone who received a council fine should seek legal advice from her organisation or Legal Aid NSW.

She also said fines were the wrong approach.

“Enforcement like this doesn’t work; you’re moving the problem somewhere else or forcing people into hiding, which puts them more at risk,” Ms Levin said.

“It’s disappointing that they’ve got to the point where council is fining people.”

Ms Levin said the problem was that there was no long-term plan for people experiencing homelessness.

“People know their only option is to move into a hotel or hide.”

Original Article published by Oliver Jacques on Region Riverina.

canberra.title: New map reveals how the new light rail corridor will be greened
canberra.snippet: More than 140 large trees will adorn the light rail route from Alinga Street to Commonwealth Park in a major planting program to green an...
canberra.content:
31 August 2026

Join the conversation

3

Commonwealth Avenue where rows of Himalayan Cedar and Chinese Elm have already been planted. Photo: Ian Bushnell.

More than 140 large trees will adorn the light rail route from Alinga Street to Commonwealth Park in a major planting program to green and soften the impacts of the $577 million project.

Canberrans can now discover where and what species have and will be planted with the publication of a new interactive map on the Built for CBR website.

The Light Rail Stage 2A Tree Plantings Map provides an interactive guide to the city’s planned urban tree canopy, including the locations of new trees, the species selected, and the environmental benefits they will provide.

The new plantings feature a mix of deciduous and evergreen species that will complement existing trees along London Circuit and Commonwealth Avenue, including Himalayan Cedars (Cedrus deodara) and Pin Oaks (Quercus palustris).

Other species to be planted are London Plane, Chinese Elm “Yarralumla”, Zelkova Green Vase or Japanese Elm, Weeping Myall, Tulip Tree and Red Spotted Gum.

Infrastructure Canberra said the trees were already growing at Yarralumla Nursery, so trees could be well advanced before being planted as part of the project. Many were standing over four metres tall.

It said the Himalayan Cedars planted along Commonwealth Avenue had been propagated from the same seedstock source as the trees south of the lake near Albert Hall planted under the direction of Charles Weston.

The more than 100-year-old Himalayan Cedars in the Commonwealth Avenue median are slated to be removed when the planned Light Rail Stage 2B to Woden alignment is constructed through the Parliamentary Zone.

On the Northbourne Avenue median between the Sydney and Melbourne Buildings, green tracks will be flanked by plantings of deciduous Green Vase Zelkova.

Along London Circuit, deciduous, climate-resistant London Plane trees will dominate. These trees were selected on the advice of the National Capital Design Review Panel to maintain a consistent streetscape and provide symmetry with the numerous other London Plane trees across the city.

The interactive map says Commonwealth Avenue’s tree selections strengthen its historic character as an elegant tree-lined boulevard.

Along the verges, there will be rows of evergreen Himalayan Cedar and deciduous Chinese Elm, while between the green tracks in the median will be a row of Pin Oaks well suited to the Canberra climate.

Small strategic stands of Tulip Trees and Red Spotted Gum round out the selections.

Infrastructure Canberra said that, once established, the new trees along Stage 2A were expected to increase tree canopy coverage along the route to more than 30 per cent, in line with the targets of the ACT Government’s Urban Forest Strategy 2021-2045.

Infrastructure Canberra said planting had already commenced on parts of the alignment, with new trees in position outside the Sydney and Melbourne Buildings, and on the Commonwealth Avenue verges.

Further planting is scheduled for later stages of the construction program.

canberra.title: Warmer winter plants seeds for a ‘cocktail’ of pollen this spring
canberra.snippet: It’s looking like it’ll be a rough start for hay fever sufferers this spring, but relief could be on the horizon. That’...
canberra.content:
31 August 2026

Start the conversation

Dr Simon Haberle is in charge of the Canberra Pollen Monitoring Centre – and he says this spring could bring a “cocktail” of pollens. Photo: James Coleman.

It’s looking like it’ll be a rough start for hay fever sufferers this spring, but relief could be on the horizon.

That’s the message from Professor Simon Haberle, director of the Canberra Pollen Monitoring Centre at the Australian National University (ANU).

He says a “cocktail” of different pollens is on the cards this spring.

When asked what it means for hay fever sufferers, Professor Haberle says it depends on the climate.

“There’s good and bad in this scenario,” he tells Region.

“This coming season – because it’s forecast as being an El Niño period – we anticipate that the grass pollen in particular will be average or below average.

“That’s good news for Canberrans … there could be quite a bit of variability.”

Professor Haberle says there could be an early peak to the circulation of grass pollens this spring.

“This year there’s a forecast for El Niño, which I think will not only bring warmer temperatures but much drier periods as well.

“We anticipate that the grass growth period will probably be stronger (early on) but the grass will die off fairly early – potentially it will reduce the impact of grass-related hay fever.”

That could mean life gets easier for hay fever sufferers and asthmatics as the year goes on.

“What we are anticipating, given the warmer temperatures … [is] that there’ll be a strong burst of grass pollen that usually starts in that last week of September to early October,” he says.

“That’s the pollen that most people suffer hay fever symptoms from.

“That could be a bit early, but we’re waiting to see what the data tells.”

Ryegrass is among the plants releasing pollen as the weather warms – and it can blow “from many tens of kilometres away into the city”. Photo: Damien Larkins.

The bush capital is also affected by “a lot” of tree pollen, including cypress pine, birch, casuarina and “a whole range of other tree types”.

Most trees will start to flower in the coming weeks, though some, like pinus and cypress pine, have already begun (you can thank them for the yellow dust on your car over the past few days).

Professor Haberle says that their pollen production is expected to continue until summertime arrives.

“Even though we’ve got a drier period, the tree can continue to produce a high degree of tree pollen,” he says.

“Unlike the grass, they don’t tend to dry off … [They’ll release] quite regular and large amounts of pollen. They’re less impacted by La Niña and El Niño, relatively, than the grasses.”

Professor Haberle predicts there will be an “average or perhaps below average risk” of Canberra recording ‘extreme’ pollen amounts this spring.

“The worst days – the most extreme pollen days – are when we have strong northwestly or westerly winds coming into Canberra.

“That’s when we see these big extreme days when people start to suffer and feel the effects of hay fever.”

Canberra Pollen posts information to its Twitter/X page on daily pollen counts and forecasts for Canberra.

australia.title: Australians missing in the Nepal floods: what we know so far
australia.snippet: There are 43 Australians among the thousands of people missing as rescue efforts continue after deadly flash floods on the Nepal-Tibet bo...
australia.content:
Pilgrims trekking to a holy site in Tibet make up the majority of Australians who have been reported missing after deadly flash floods and landslides tore through valleys on the Nepal-Tibet border on Wednesday.

The total number of Australians missing in the disaster rose to 43 on Monday, with most travelling with Himalayan Glacier Adventures, Kailash Journeys, and the Isha Foundation.

Cara Severino, 25, is no longer included in the figure after the Sydney woman made contact with her parents, two days after she was reported missing.

Across Nepal and Tibet, thousands of people have been reported missing and Nepali and Chinese authorities have confirmed hundreds have died.

Here’s what we know about the Australians who remain missing. This article will be updated as more information becomes available.

Venkatraman Balakrishnan and Chitra Venkatraman

New South Wales couple Venkatraman Balakrishnan, 52, and Chitra Venkatraman, 46, were among 15 Australians travelling to Mount Kailash on a spiritual trip with the Himalayan Glacier Adventures tour group.

Their son, Akash Venkatraman, said his parents planned to leave their riverside accommodation in Syabrubesi before it was devastated by flood waters.

Muralitharan family

Shylaja Muralitharan, 42, Chandresekaran Muralitharan, 47 and their children Ashwin, 14, and Aarush, 11, were also taking part in the Himalayan Glacier Adventures spiritual tour to Mount Kailash when the flood hit.

The parents and two children had been training together for the long walk, Shylaja’s younger sister, Vaishnavi, said.

She had lost contact with the family shortly after breakfast on the morning of the flood.

Iyer family

Sreedharan Iyer, 52, and Lakshmi Iyer, 50, and their adult sons Rishab Iyer, 23, and Rudhra Iyer, 20, were taking part in the spiritual pilgrimage to Mount Kailash with Himalayan Glacier Adventures.

The Iyer brothers are medical students at the University of Newcastle and members of the West Pennant Hills Cherrybrook Cricket Club in Sydney’s north-west.

Karan Bhardwaj

Karan Bhardwaj is a 40-year-old Brisbane-based member of the Royal Australian Air Force.

“Karan is a dad to my beautiful seven-year-old nephew, as well as a brother, uncle and brother in law,” said his family member Jen. “He is so desperately loved by his family and right now we are desperately praying, hoping and believing that Karan is safe, alive and somehow making his way back to us.”

Narayan Panthi

Narayan Panthi, from Brisbane, has been listed by Nepali police as travelling with operator Kathmandu Holiday Tours and Travel. It is understood Panthi had been carrying out independent volunteer charity work in Kathmandu earlier in the week before travelling towards the border region.

Panthi’s cousin, Amrit Bhusal, told Guardian Australia his family were devastated but “holding on to hope and praying for positive news”.

“We are still hoping,” Bhusal said. “We are still searching. We are still praying for Narayan to come home safely.”

Bhusal said Panthi was “helping disadvantaged children in Nepal reach their full potential through education”.

Bharat Mangwani

Bharat Mangwani, 42, was travelling with the Isha Foundation as part of a pilgrimage to Lake Manasarovar when his family lost contact with him on Wednesday morning.

He was last seen at Gyirong before the group was set to depart for Kathmandu.

“All of us are praying for him and hopefully he comes back to us soon,” close friend Kushagra Tiwari said.

Mangwani’s family, including his nine-year-old son and three-year-old daughter, have travelled to India with a family friend, while his wife has flown to Nepal to look for him.

Sumi Adhikari

Sumi Adhikari, 41, was at the Gyirong Port crossing with the Isha Foundation group when the flood hit.

Her husband, Nava Pandey, has travelled to Nepal seeking information about her whereabouts.

“We still have no clear or official information about Sumi or the other members of her group,” Pandey said on Saturday morning.

Renee Spry

A Sunshine Coast disability support worker, Renee Spry has been described as a “deeply spiritual” person who travelled to Nepal on a pilgrimage.

“She had two degrees, and she chose to do something that was … a completely selfless vocation. Her priority was always other people,” her sister Clair Spry said.

“Every person she touched, they knew her love and kindness. She would be so uncomfortable with all this.”

Clair Spry has set up a GoFundMe so her family can travel to Nepal to look for signs of Renee.

Suhasini Kandimalla

A mother of two from Springfield, near Brisbane, Suhasini Kandimalla was hiking with another Springfield local, according to her sister, Supreethini Kandimalla.

While she was a New Zealand citizen, Suhasini had been approved for Australian citizenship, her sister said. She had planned to attend a citizenship ceremony for it to be granted soon after she returned.

“I don’t know if it was a religious calling for her to do it,” Supreethini said of the Nepal trip.

“But she certainly loved the treks in New Zealand too, and would go on lots of long hikes.”

Reshma Patel

Newcastle woman Reshma Patel, 46, was in the Isha Foundation group. She didn’t know Sumi Adhikari beforehand, but the pair had become friends on the pilgrimage, Patel’s family friend Chin Valsan says.

“They were talking to each other, and they were supposed to come back on the same flight on Thursday,” he says.

He describes Patel, who has two children aged 10 and 14 and works casually for Canterbury-Bankstown council, as “full of life” and a “kind soul” who loves her family and friends.

Kanagamah Sundrasan

The mother of two from Springfield, near Brisbane, was part of the Kailash Journey trek to Mount Kailash.

Her daughter, Swaatika Kanniah, said her mother had been excited about the hike.

“It was a pilgrimage, she really wanted to go and have that experience.”

A photograph of her on the trip shows her smiling with five other members of the tour; all are now missing.

“I feel like everyone is trying their best, but yes we don’t know much about what’s going on,” Kanniah said of the recovery efforts.

Michael Keats

The family of Keats said on social media he had died.

Keats’s wife, Emily Boyd, said on Instagram on Sunday that he had been on a pilgrimage to Mount Kailash, which had been his “dream for many years”.

“Mike went on a pilgrimage to Mt Kailash seeking enlightenment,” Boyd said.

“There’s a bittersweetness knowing that there was nothing more that Mike wanted [than] to know God, and to merge with the divine.

“He was a mystic, a medicine man, a teacher, leader, partner, father, brother, son, uncle and dearly beloved friend. He showed up for so many people in so many ways. A heart of pure gold. We love you forever and always.”

    Number of Australians missing in Nepal rises to 43

  • 17h ago

    Good morning

What we learned today, Monday 31 August

That’s where we’ll leave our live coverage for the day.

Before we go, let’s recap the top headlines:

  • The total number of Australians missing in the deadly Nepal floods is now 43. The death toll from the ⁠unprecedented deluge of ice, rock, mud ​and debris that crashed through valleys of Nepal on Wednesday last week has now risen to 903 people, with 16 more dead reported on the Tibet side of the border. More than 4,000 are missing in Nepal, with another 500 in Tibet.

  • Oscar Jenkins, an Australian man who was captured and sentenced to 13 years in a Russian jail after fighting for Ukraine military, has given his first interview after his conviction. The Australian government said it is working with Russian officials in a bid to secure his release.

  • One Nation’s Barnaby Joyce said the party wouldn’t get “carried away” after claiming a victory in the Secret Harbour state byelection in Western Australia.

  • According to snowfall data compiled by Snowy Hydro, 2026 is officially the worst end to a season since records began in 1954.

  • The NSW opposition leader, Kellie Sloane, says she has written to Anthony Albanese about the need to tackle violent pornography after a 16-year-old girl died from a suspected sexual strangulation incident.

  • Federal attorney general Michelle Rowland says the government is not immediately planning to ban imports of smartglasses.

  • Queensland has become the first state to make ebike and e-scooter riders hold at least a learner driver’s licence.

  • The New South Wales government will not appeal a supreme court judge’s ruling that rejected the state’s request for a terror order over Mohommed Farhat, who wrote “Fuk Israel” on cars and set another vehicle alight in late 2024.

  • New South Wales police have appealed for information to find the mother of a newborn baby boy, whose body was discovered in a rubbish bin in Auburn in Sydney’s south-west on Monday morning.

  • Qantas ground handling crews may soon walk off the job after overwhelmingly voting in favour of taking industrial action to demand better pay and conditions.

Thanks for sticking around, we’ll see you tomorrow morning.

Police appeal for mother to come forward after newborn’s body found in Sydney bin

NSW police have called on the mother of an abandoned newborn to come forward after the baby’s body was found in Sydney’s south-west today.

Emergency services were called to the suburb of Auburn after reports that a baby had been found in a bin. Officers attended and discovered the body of a baby boy.

It is believed the child was born within the last 36 hours.

Police have appealed for the unidentified mother to “come forward” or “go immediately to your closest hospital and seek treatment”.

Speaking on 2GB, Auburn police’s Acting Supt Darren Sly said:

Our main focus this afternoon, our priority, is to locate the mother of this child just to ensure that she receives the necessary medical assistance and any other welfare services that she may need.

And of course, we’re also calling for any members of the public who may have been in Harrow Road in the last 36 hours as well … all the small bits of information can be pieced together to hopefully track down this mother.

Qantas ground crews vote for right to strike amid pay dispute with airline

Catie McLeod

Qantas ground handling crews may soon walk off the job after overwhelmingly voting in favour of taking industrial action to demand better pay and conditions.

The Transport Workers’ Union (TWU) says 97% of its members employed by Qantas Ground Services (QGS) workers voted for the right to strike in the coming weeks.

QGS is a subsidiary company owned by the airline, set up when Alan Joyce was still its CEO, which – according to the union – pays workers less than its “legacy” workforce.

Its ground crews also perform work for Qantas Freight and the company’s regional Q-Link service, the union says.

The TWU says its health and safety reps in New South Wales have served Qantas with 14 provisional improvement notices over alleged safety failings at Qantas Freight, where a labour hire worker died last year.

The workers voted to strike less than a week after Qantas reported its financial results for the last year, revealing it may hike fares after its profits dipped to a four-year low. The TWU national secretary, Michael Kaine, said:

Last week we saw Qantas crying poor over $2bn in profits, while the board awarded itself a 17% pay rise – but workers and the public see right through it.

These ground workers don’t want to go on strike, but after being sold a false promise that this airline would finally treat them with respect, they’ve got no other choice.

A Qantas spoksperson said:

We remain committed to reaching an agreement with our Qantas Ground Services employees that includes annual pay rises for our people.

We have well developed contingency plans to minimise any impact on customers and our operations, should we be notified of any industrial action.

Discussions through the Fair Work Commission have been constructive and negotiations are continuing.

Liberal shadow minister calls Hanson hypocritical over accusations Labor is inflaming political discourse

The assistant shadow minister for energy, Garth Hamilton, has called One Nation leader Pauline Hanson’s accusation – that the government was “pouring petrol” on inflamed political discourse – hypocritical.

It comes after the One Nation leader accused the prime minister and the treasurer of being “dangerous, divisive and downright dishonest”.

Speaking on ABC’s Afternoon Briefing, Hamilton said:

Senator Hanson has made a career going on Sky News after dark saying much worse things. I’m sure there’s a Labor strategist trawling through the comments she’s made that’s been more strongly worded than ‘dangerous, divisive’ and whatever else it was.

I think there’s a bit of hypocrisy at play. This constant game of I’m the victim. I would remind everybody this is a party that by its own admission is currently infiltrated by extremists.

This is absolutely nonsense, it’s not right. Hypocrisy should be called hypocrisy, and that’s what this is.

Nick Visser

That’s all for me! Achol Arok will take things from here.

Lisa Cox

NSW may not be able to prosecute large-scale water theft

The New South Wales water regulator has cast doubt over its ability to prosecute potential water theft due to uncertainty about the validity of licences governing billions of litres of water entitlements in the state’s north.

It follows a successful legal challenge brought by a group of irrigators in the state’s north-west which found 11 floodplain harvesting licences issued by the former Coalition government were invalid.

The NSW land and environment court found the government had failed to follow correct procedures related to fair consultation with landholders. The case, known as Emu Rider, has raised questions about the validity of the process used to issue hundreds of floodplain harvesting licences.

Read more:

NSW police appeal for information after body of newborn found in Sydney

NSW police are appealing for information after the body of a newborn baby was found in Sydney’s south-west today.

Officials said emergency services were called to the suburb of Auburn amid reports the baby had been found in a bin. Officers attended and discovered the body of a baby boy.

Police have established a crime scene and commenced an investigation.

They hold serious concerns for the welfare of the baby’s mother and are urging her to attend the nearest hospital to receive urgent care. Police are also asking for anyone with information about the incident, or who was in the area at the time with any relevant footage, to contact police.

Kids leaning into AI as literacy levels decline

A majority of Australian youth lack confidence distinguishing news fact from fiction as they increasingly source information from artificial intelligence, AAP reports.

The 2026 News and Young Australians Report, released on Monday, found just 47% of children aged between 10 and 17 felt confident they could spot disinformation online.

A third of the 1,027 kids surveyed had shared a news story on social media to later find it was false.

Data showed youths were less likely to take steps to verify news content than in 2023’s study. Those steps included discussing items, checking multiple stories and changing news sources to more trustworthy outlets.

Declining literacy coincided with increased use of artificial intelligence, the survey also found.

Hanson says Albanese and Chalmers ‘crossed a line’ over criticisms of One Nation

One Nation’s leader, Pauline Hanson, said Anthony Albanese and treasurer Jim Chalmers had “crossed a line” after the prime minister said the party was “peddling politics” that are “dangerous, divisive and downright dishonest” during Queensland’s Labor conference.

Hanson took to social media, writing today:

No matter how worried Jim and Albanese are about losing their jobs, telling Australians that their democratically elected opponents are “dangerous” and a “threat to our country” invites people to treat them as a threat.

Words have consequences. That is how political violence is incited.

The One Nation leader went on to say the pair were “pouring petrol” over inflamed political discourse, warning:

The real danger to Jim and Albanese is that the people of Australia are coming for their government … at the ballot box.

Caitlin Cassidy

Continuing on from the last post …

The judge criticised the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance (IHRA) definition of antisemitism as “detached from the reality of the common usage and understanding of antisemitism in this country”.

Australia’s peak Jewish group labelled Fagan’s ruling dangerous judicial “activism” that should be reviewed.

Greens MP Sue Higginson on Monday said:

It was bewildering to see the Minns Labor government signalling they would appeal this decision.

The government’s own legal experts have clearly seen the writing on the wall and told the attorney general that any appeal of this decision would fail.

NSW will not appeal ruling that found anti-Israel vandalism was not antisemitic

Caitlin Cassidy

The New South Wales government will not appeal a supreme court judge’s ruling that rejected the state’s request for a terror order over Mohommed Farhat, who wrote “Fuk Israel” on cars and set another vehicle alight in late 2024.

Last week, Guardian Australia reported that the government was “seeking urgent advice” on the prospects of any appeal after Justice Desmond Fagan had found that disparaging Israel was “political comment”, not antisemitism.

On Monday, the NSW attorney general, Michael Daley, told a budget estimates hearing “we won’t be appealing that decision”.

“Having considered the advice from the crown solicitor, senior and junior counsel, I have reached the conclusion that an appeal would have no reasonable prospects and would fail,” Daley said.

The individual is serving a 20-month sentence in relation to his prior offending and remains in custody.

In his ruling earlier this month, Fagan ruled that police, lower courts and various state agencies all incorrectly labelled Farhat’s actions antisemitic, meaning he was treated more harshly.

Queensland becomes first state to mandate licence requirements for ebikes and e-scooters

From Monday, Queensland has become the first state to make ebike and e-scooter riders hold at least a learner driver’s licence, with new rules kicking in on top of age limits and a statewide police blitz seizing hundreds of non-compliant devices, AAP reports.

Riders must now have a valid learner’s licence to use electric-powered cycles and e-scooters on Queensland roads and paths, with limited exemptions for supervised 12 to 17-year-olds, medically exempt riders and people in designated off-road recreation areas.

“We always said we would make the tough decisions to keep the community safe; our laws get the balance right between cracking down on those who do the wrong thing, while backing those Queenslanders who do the right thing and delivering sensible exemptions,” the state transport minister, Brent Mickelberg, said.

Police have already issued more than 1,700 fines and seized almost 400 illegal devices since 1 July under Operation Yankee Surety, and will now start checking licences during street intercepts.

It is now almost certain the world will warm past 1.5C. But ‘net-negative’ emissions are still possible

Wesley Morgan for the Conversation has written about the greatest threat to the Pacific: climate change.

Anthony Albanese is in Palau this week for the annual Pacific Islands Forum and regional security is expected to top the agenda.

China is testing nuclear-capable missiles in the Pacific, prompting talk of a new regional agreement. The United States-Iran war has exposed a reliance on costly fossil fuels that is undermining Pacific economies.

And as the world comes perilously close to the Paris agreement’s 1.5C temperature goal, a record-breaking El Niño looms in the Pacific Ocean.

Pacific nations will want Albanese to address the world’s key security threat – climate change. As president of negotiations of the Cop31 climate talks in November, Australia can work with the Pacific to keep 1.5C within reach and secure much-needed finance for island nations at the climate frontline.

Read more here:

Government not planning to ban import of smartglasses, says Rowland

Luca Ittimani

Michelle Rowland says the government is not immediately planning to ban imports of smartglasses.

The Greens and others have called for the camera-enabled wearable technology to locked out of the country.

The attorney general has told reporters the calls to limit the technology were “valid”. She said:

Firstly, I want to acknowledge the very deep concerns. We are not specifically in this consultation consulting on an import ban. … that would have consequences across government, including across trade, foreign affairs, and other potential legal obligations that can apply internationally.

She said the government’s reforms today would still impact on the smartglasses, with digital platforms prevented from storing recordings and data from the glasses if it was not “fair and reasonable” to do so.

Rowland said she commended local governments who were blocking the glasses’ use, for example at public pools, and said the federal government needed to use the powers that it had.

Let’s be clear, we’re talking about the harmful behaviours and regulating the harms. That’s what governments seek to do. In terms of an import ban, as I said, we are not ruling anything out, but we are utilising what we have at our disposal right now.

Attorney general outlines planned privacy reforms including 'right to erasure'

Luca Ittimani

The attorney general, Michelle Rowland, is announcing planned new privacy reforms at a Canberra press conference. She has told reporters:

We know that Australians are increasingly concerned about how their data is being collected, used, and shared, particularly as AI and other emerging technologies such as smart glasses become more accessible. People should not have to choose between protecting their privacy and participating in the digital economy.

She said the government was planning to introduce:

  • A “fair and reasonable” test to limit companies to collecting and using only the personal information they need;

  • A right to erasure, so people can ask digital platforms to destroy their stores of personal information;

  • Stronger standards for consent and clearer information when people agree to share personal details;

  • Limits on businesses buying and selling personal information without clear permission;

  • And a new ID Lock service through MyGov, designed to let Australians block, unblock, and monitor the use of their eligible identity documents for verification.

Benita Kolovos

Victorian prisoners to be sent out to repair roads under Labor’s pothole plan

Victorian prisoners will be put to work on road maintenance as part of Labor’s plan to fix the state’s potholes if re-elected.

The state’s premier, Ben Carroll, will outline the plan on Monday off the back of an announcement on Sunday that the government would be increasing the road maintenance budget by $352m to fix 500,000 potholes by the end of January.

Carroll will declare that if Labor wins the November election, it would work with Corrections Victoria to develop a pilot program to put supervised, minimum-security prisoners to work performing roadside maintenance.

The plan would include having inmates take over “basic” duties such as mowing lawns, controlling weeds, removing graffiti and picking up rubbish, allowing more skilled crews to focus on fixing potholes.

The government said the work of prisoners “will not replace paid jobs” but instead “supplement the workforce where there are skill and capacity shortages”.

Read more here:

australia.title: Newborn baby’s body found in Sydney rubbish bin as police hold ‘serious concerns’ for mother
australia.snippet: Police urge mother to attend hospital after baby’s body discovered in Harrow Road in Auburn Follow our Australia news live blog for lates...
australia.content:
New South Wales police have appealed for information to find the mother of a newborn baby boy, whose body was discovered in a rubbish bin in Auburn in Sydney’s west on Monday morning.

Police said emergency services responded to reports of the body of a baby located in a rubbish bin at a unit block along Harrow Road in Auburn at 11.20am, with officers from the Auburn police area command finding the body of a newborn boy.

Acting superintendent of the Auburn area police command, Darren Sly, told reporters that the baby’s body was discovered by a local resident putting out the rubbish.

The baby was unclothed and was in a plastic rubbish bag, Sly said.

“It’s a sad set of circumstances,” Sly said.

“Our number one priority and our number one concern is that of the mother.”

A crime scene has been established and detectives have commenced an investigation into the incident.

Police said they hold “serious concerns” for the welfare of the baby’s mother, and have urged the mother to attend the nearest hospital to receive urgent care.

Sly told 2GB radio it was believed the baby was born in the past 36 hours, but the body will need to be examined more thoroughly.

Anyone with more information about the incident, or who was in the area at the time and may have dashcam or mobile footage relevant to the incident, are urged to contact Auburn police station or Crime Stoppers on 1800 333 000.

Sly said police were door-knocking in the area and looking for CCTV.

“All the small bits of information can obviously piece together to hopefully track down this mother,” he said.

“I appeal to the mother to come forward, to go immediately to your closest hospital and seek treatment.”

australia.title: Man who murdered Molly Ticehurst unlikely to face life in jail, court hears
australia.snippet: Justice Natalie Adams says she is troubled by expert evidence about rape allegations in slain woman’s police statement Follow our Austral...
australia.content:
Molly Ticehurst’s ex-boyfriend is unlikely to face a life sentence for her domestic violence murder, a crime which galvanised a national movement against gendered abuse.

Ticehurst, a 28-year-old childcare educator, was found dead in her home at Forbes, in the New South Wales central-west, in the early hours of 22 April 2024.

Her former boyfriend Daniel Billings broke into her bedroom and stabbed her 15 times in a ferocious attack that lasted less than a minute.

Billings had been charged with several counts of raping Ticehurst and a string of domestic violence offences just over two weeks before the killing, but he was freed on bail by a local court registrar the next day.

Ticehurst’s death became a flashpoint in the nation’s fight against domestic violence and led to legal changes in NSW, including tighter bail laws.

Billings, 31, who has pleaded guilty to murder, is will face court in Orange for a two-day sentence hearing from Thursday.

During a mention in the NSW supreme court on Monday, Adams raised the issue of a life sentence, although she noted she did not expect it to be requested.

Crown submissions before the court do not seek a life term, but they argue Billings should not get any discount on his sentence because his level of culpability is “extreme”.

Adams said there would probably be mitigating factors to consider when sentencing Billings, as there were in almost all cases.

“It’s difficult to identify what’s [legally] unique about this case,” she said.

But the judge said she was troubled with how to deal with expert evidence about Ticehurst’s police statement that she was repeatedly raped by Billings.

The sexual assault charges were dropped when Billings pleaded guilty to murder in November 2025 after 18 months of legal negotiations.

Billings always denied raping Ticehurst and developed a dark obsession with clearing his name in the lead-up to the murder.

“If I’m going to do the time, I may as well do the crime,” he said in a conversation with a friend soon before the murder, according to a statement of agreed facts before the court.

Adams said she could not ignore the rape allegations, despite the charges being dropped, when it came to sentencing Billings for murder.

“It was him seeing the police facts that set him to spiral,” the judge said.

Acting out of spite over the allegations could push his crime into another serious category, she said.

“The sense of grievance about a perceived false allegation, there’s no getting around that,” Adams said.

“Whether it’s almost a public-justice type murder or domestic-violence type murder.”

Adams said it was possible all the elements to satisfy the legal definition of sexual assault were in Ticehurst’s account to police.

Changes to consent laws in NSW, which included affirmative language in the legislation, meant it was a crime where both parties “feel they’re telling the truth”.

“The only witness who could have told us is dead,” the judge said.

Billings, who has been in custody in the supermax wing of Goulburn jail since he was charged, will face court in person.

He will hear victim impact statements from the Ticehurst family, along with expert evidence about his mental state at the time of the murder.

A series of videos he made before and after the murder are also expected to be played to court.

Ticehurst’s death became a flashpoint in the nation’s fight against domestic violence and led to legal changes in NSW, including tighter bail laws.

Adams has indicated she will sentence Billings later in September.

australia.title: Afternoon Update: One Nation’s nuclear plans; on the ground in Nepal; and $100 chicken nuggets
australia.snippet: Want to get this in your inbox every weekday? Sign up for the Afternoon Update here , and start your day with our Morning Mail newsletter...
australia.content:
Good afternoon.

Pauline Hanson says two nuclear reactors should be built on Australia’s east coast, in remarks at odds with One Nation’s official policy.

Speaking in Victoria ahead of the November state election, the One Nation leader said “the reactors need to happen”, while also calling for taxpayer funding to keep coal-fired Loy Yang power station outside Traralgon operating, as part of a push for a “diversity” of power supply.

Hanson insists the policy is nothing like Peter Dutton’s failed push to build plants during his unsuccessful election campaign.

The party’s own official policy calls for $6.8bn to be spent on construction of one east coast nuclear reactor, to be built at a site supported by community consultation.

Top news

  • Man who murdered Molly Ticehurst will not face life in jail, judge says

  • Victorian prisoners to be sent out to repair roads under Labor’s pothole plan

  • ‘It was like fighting a dinosaur’: Sydney shark attack survivor recalls left hook that helped save her life

  • Icac lawyer tells Charles Perrottet the key to lying is ‘you have to be really good at remembering it’

  • Newborn baby’s body found in Sydney rubbish bin as police hold ‘serious concerns’ for mother

  • NSW may not be able to prosecute large-scale water theft due to doubts about licences for billions of litres

In pictures

Guardian Australia’s Cait Kelly is reporting from Nepal as the country continues to reckon with the humanitarian crisis caused by Nepal-Tibet flood disaster.

The first thing Kelly noticed is the noise: “Chopper blades cutting through the air as helicopters come and go from the main army response centre, at the entrance to Nepal’s flood zone. Then, there is the smell. A putrid, iodine smell. Blood and bone. The severe heat beating down on bodies packed into white bags – being carried off in helicopters and laid in an area so families can identify them.”

You can read more of her reporting here, and read everything we know so far about the Australians still missing in Nepal.

What they said …

“These algorithms prey on people.” – Kellie Sloane

 The NSW opposition leader says she has written to Anthony Albanese after a 16-year-old girl died from a suspected sexual strangulation incident.

Sloane said certain types of pornography should be placed into the most restricted category and pressure should be applied on porn companies and social media giants to “just make sure wherever we’re at, we can block it”. 

Podcast

On the ground in decimated Nepal flood zone

Rescue efforts are continuing in Nepal and Tibet after flash floods that have killed hundreds and left many more missing. But fears that a lake formed by the landslide could overflow and cause fresh flooding, along with difficulty accessing disaster-hit areas, are hindering rescue and recovery missions.

Lucy Hough speaks with south Asia correspondent Hannah Ellis-Petersen, who is in Nepal, about the situation on the ground.

You can listen here, and watch on YouTube here.

Before bed read

How did the US Open become obscenely expensive? Record crowds, $100 chicken nuggets and an unchecked resale market are transforming the self-styled people’s slam – and leaving ordinary fans fighting to get through the gates.

Daily word game

Today’s starter word is: MUSE. You have five goes to get the longest word including the starter word. Play Wordiply.

If you would like to receive this Afternoon Update to your email inbox every weekday, sign up here, or start your day with a curated breakdown of the key stories you need to know with our Morning Mail newsletter. You can follow the latest in US politics by signing up for This Week in Trumpland.

world.title: Countries legally obliged to consider slavery reparations, says UN committee
world.snippet: Guidance says states must implement ‘comprehensive measures’ to address legacy of racial discrimination A UN committee has said countries...
world.content:
A UN committee has said countries are legally obliged to consider reparations for the transatlantic slave trade and take other ⁠measures to address the enduring ⁠legacy of racial ​discrimination.

Guidance published on Monday by the committee on the elimination of racial discrimination (CERD) said the obligations arose from ⁠a legally binding 1965 convention on racial discrimination, not from the legal standards that existed when the slave trade took place.

The committee described the approach as a “paradigm ⁠shift” away from debates over historical responsibility that have often been used by governments to resist reparations ​claims.

“States parties must implement comprehensive reparatory measures for ‌people of African descent, ‌covering all aspects of remedies,” said the UN document, which may be cited in courtrooms.

At least 12.5 ‌million Africans were taken and sold between the 15th and 19th centuries in what CERD called the largest forced displacement in history.

Calls for reparations – ranging from official apologies to financial compensation – have gained momentum internationally, though opponents argue states and institutions should not be held responsible for historical crimes. The EU and Britain abstained from a UN resolution ‌on slavery in March.

Some states have sought to dodge claims for justice in courtrooms by arguing that there were no international laws outlawing the slave trade ​at the time – the so-called intertemporality principle.

But the UN document argues that, regardless of whether slavery and the slave trade were illegal under the laws of the day, countries remain responsible under current international obligations to tackle their continuing effects.

“Irrespective of the legal characterisation of the original historical acts, states parties remain bound ⁠by their present obligations under the convention to address structural inequalities,” the UN document ​says.

Financial compensation alone is ​not sufficient, it adds, urging “transformative” measures including ​opening archives, revising public memorials and establishing independent truth commissions.

Pela Boker Wilson, a committee expert ​from Liberia who helped draft ‌the document, said ​she expected states ​to move beyond broad expressions of regret and review policies and laws.

“We are calling on state parties to take concrete and meaningful action,” she told Reuters. “We want to affirm the dignity of those whose suffering was denied, whose suffering was minimised or forgotten.”

world.title: Morocco not to blame for Ceuta border breach, says Spanish PM
world.snippet: Pedro Sánchez says two countries cooperating and accuses Israel and Russia of spreading fake news about migration Spain’s prime minister,...
world.content:
Spain’s prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, has said there is no evidence to suggest the Moroccan government was behind last month’s massive border crossing into Ceuta but accused Israel and Russia of spreading disinformation.

As many as 141 people are thought to have died trying to enter the Spanish enclave at the end of July. The influx of about 70,000 men, women and children unleashed a political crisis, a humanitarian emergency and reignited tensions within the EU over immigration.

Despite speculation that Rabat may have engineered the mass crossing as a means of showing its displeasure at Spain’s rapprochement with Algeria, Sánchez said there was nothing to indicate the involvement of the Moroccan authorities.

“There’s no information from any intelligence agency that raises doubts over the involvement of Moroccan authorities,” he told Cadena Ser radio on Monday. “Cooperation with Morocco is frankly positive. I’d like to stress that we need to be aware that this crisis can be resolved only through cooperation – and not through a lack of trust in Morocco, which would only further aggravate the already complex situation we have in Ceuta.”

Sánchez said fake news had been pumped out on social media accounts “associated with Russia, Israel and the international far right that always use migration to attack not just Spain but also Europe”.

The accusation drew a furious response from Israel. The country’s foreign minister, Gideon Sa’ar, called it a “brazen lie”, adding: “Continuing to spread defamatory lies will not distract from Sánchez’s disgraceful failure to manage his country’s affairs.”

The ⁠Kremlin rejected allegations ⁠that ​Russia was connected to ⁠the Ceuta migration crisis, the ⁠RBC daily ​reported ‌on ‌Monday.

Sánchez repeated his assertion that the influx was due to the activities of “criminal gangs” who had used disinformation to falsely claim that a ruling by Spain’s supreme court meant that no one who entered Ceuta by swimming could be deported back to Morocco.

Although the overwhelming majority of the migrants crossed back into Morocco weeks ago, at least 1,500 people, including minors, are still on the streets of Ceuta. Their continuing presence has led to clashes between some Ceuta residents and police, while some of the migrants have had their belongings burned while sleeping rough on beaches. On Saturday, four Moroccan migrants were arrested for throwing stones at Spanish soldiers.

Sánchez said there would soon be “sufficient capacity” to accommodate all those still in the enclave.

Spain’s conservative People’s party has accused the government of failing to protect the people of Ceuta. “It did nothing to avoid the invasion on 30 July and it’s doing nothing to stop the public order crisis that’s getting worse every day,” the PP’s leader, Alberto Núñez Feijóo, said last week.

Santiago Abascal, the leader of the far-right Vox party, has described events in Ceuta as “an invasion and an act of war promoted by Morocco and allowed by Sánchez, who is incapable of responding because he is subservient to Morocco”.

world.title: People fleeing Sudan civil war face ‘dire and deteriorating’ conditions in refuge city
world.snippet: More traumatised civilians are arriving every day at ‘shockingly overcrowded’ El Obeid and camps on its outskirts Humanitarian conditions...
world.content:
Humanitarian conditions in the Sudanese city of El Obeid and two camps on its outskirts are dire and deteriorating, according to people on the ground, as civilians displaced by fighting between the Sudanese Armed Forces and Rapid Support Forces (RSF) militia continue to pour in from the surrounding countryside.

The UN says more than 15,000 families have arrived since mid-July, joining more than 200,000 people who arrived in the first half of the year, according to government figures cited by Save the Children.

“The situation is very harsh and is deteriorating as El Obeid is receiving IDPs [internally displaced people] on a daily basis … The city is shockingly overcrowded,” said Maryam, a humanitarian volunteer whose name has been changed for her safety.

The new arrivals came on foot, carrying almost nothing, she said. “They also suffer from a shortage of food and they definitely arrive traumatised.”

The city, the capital of North Kordofan province, was home to around half a million people before the war broke out more than three years ago.

While many of the new arrivals have been absorbed into the city, tens of thousands are living in two main tented camps. According to analysis of satellite data by the Yale Humanitarian Research Lab, 800 new tents appeared in one of the camps between 4 and 25 August.

“During my visit, I saw 450 arrivals coming from the surrounding villages just that morning,” said Paul Byars, the Sudan country director for the Danish Refugee Council, who was in El Obeid last week. “The authorities’ estimates are correct, that 85% of them are women and children. Most of the men are staying behind because this is the only time for farming.”

Civil war erupted in Sudan’s capital, Khartoum, about 250 miles (400km) north-east of El Obeid, on 15 April 2023, when a power struggle between the armed forces and RSF descended into open conflict.

Since then, about 11.3 million people have been displaced, more than a fifth of the population. Some parts of the country, including El Obeid and surrounding areas, are at risk of famine.

Estimates of the number of people killed in the war range from tens to hundreds of thousands. More than 10,000 people are thought to have been massacred by the RSF in El Fasher over two days when they seized the city in Sudan’s western Darfur region in October 2025 after an 18-month siege.

A surge in RSF drone strikes on El Obeid and nearby areas in June led the UN to warn that the city could face a repeat of what happened in El Fasher.

The number of strikes has since fallen. The armed forces also recaptured a key road leading north to Khartoum in late July, which at least partly lifted the threat of besiegement. However, drones are still killing and injuring civilians, while violence rages in the surrounding districts, pushing people to the city.

Recently, volunteers in El Obeid had noticed more “double-tap” drone strikes, where a second drone follows the first, hitting rescuers at the scene, Maryam said. “It is hard, so hard, living with this, hearing the sound of a drone hitting somewhere,” she said. “It’s very disturbing.”

Sudan’s civil war has become dominated by drones, accounting for half of all violent incidents, up from 4% at the start of the war, said Nohad Eltayeb, who monitors Sudan for Acled, a conflict tracking group.

Both sides used drones, but the RSF’s usage had become more volatile since the US war with Iran began to interrupt supply lines in February, she said. “They rely on fewer, very targeted strikes.”

So far this year, there have been 322 incidents of violence affecting civilians in the wider Kordofan region, compared with 388 for the whole of 2025, according to Acled data. While the RSF was responsible for half of those, the SAF has also killed and injured civilians. On 10 August, armed forces and an allied militia killed five civilians and injured 10 about 60 miles north-east of El Obeid, according to Emergency Lawyers, a non-governmental group.

With the threats to delivery trucks, food prices have rocketed. In north Kordofan in July, according to World Food Programme data, a litre of groundnut oil cost 17,000 Sudanese pounds (£21), up from 13,000 in June and 7,700 a year ago. The prices of wheat flour and goat and sheep meat have also more than doubled in the last year.

Meanwhile, El Obeid’s power and water infrastructure still has not fully recovered from RSF drone strikes in June.

“The main problem is the big [water] source that is in the north of the city has been severely damaged and it has not been repaired,” said Esperanza Santos, an emergency coordinator in Sudan for Médecins Sans Frontières. “The water pipes in the city have [also] been impacted. So mostly, both in the city – for example, in the hospital – and also in the IDP camps, they are relying on water trucking and it’s not enough.”

Conditions in the camps were poor too, Santos said. “In terms of sanitation, it’s very, very bad. It’s not enough. The ratio of latrines per person is impossible – there are more than 100 people for a latrine. So basically there is open defecation.”

Maryam said she and her fellow local volunteers remained committed, despite the difficulties. “The situation is deteriorating, but we are trying to stay together, to stay strong in the face of the drone attacks and the influx of IDPs … We are living with this and we hope things will become better.”

world.title: Egyptian queen’s 673-diamond necklace stolen in Vienna smash-and-grab raid
world.snippet: Police hunt two suspects after historic 200-carat piece is snatched from Austrian museum during opening hours Austrian police are hunting...
world.content:
Austrian police are hunting two men alleged to have stolen a 200-carat platinum necklace encrusted with 673 diamonds that was on loan to a museum in Vienna and once belonged to Egyptian royalty.

Authorities in the capital released pictures of the suspects captured by security cameras during the heist at the Museum of Applied Arts (MAK), amid a rash of spectacular smash-and-grab thefts from European cultural institutions.

The unmasked men bought tickets to the exhibition before shattering a glass display case with a hammer during opening hours on Thursday afternoon and making off with the diamond necklace.

In an appeal for information from the public, police said: “The perpetrators fled with the jewellery in an unknown direction.”

Officers fanned out through the city centre and deployed a police tracking dog to search for the suspects. The Kronen newspaper said investigators believed the men were probably carrying out a “contract job” on behalf of a criminal gang.

MAK said the piece had been snatched from a jewellery exhibition that had been on display since June, featuring more than 300 works by the French designers Van Cleef & Arpels. No one was hurt, although there were several witnesses in the room at the time.

Documentation for the show said the necklace once belonged to Queen Consort Nazli of Egypt, who wore it at the 1939 wedding of her daughter Fawzia to Iran’s then crown prince, Mohammad Reza Pahlavi, who later became shah. The necklace was sold by Sotheby’s in New York in 2015 for $4.3m.

The MAK said the exhibition brought together about 200 “unique and rarely seen objects” from its own collection and pieces spanning the 120-year history of the Parisian jewellery house, from the Van Cleef & Arpels patrimonial collection.

A guided tour planned for Friday afternoon was listed as “cancelled” on the museum website and the exhibition, which was due to end on 27 September, was temporarily closed.

European museums have been hit by a string of high-profile heists since thieves broke into the Louvre museum in Paris during the day last October and escaped within minutes with crown jewels worth €88m.

In Spain on Thursday, thieves raided the Treasure of Villena, a collection of bronze age gold artefacts described as one of Europe’s most important prehistoric hoards.

This month, four of the most important works by the 15th-century Renaissance master Antonello da Messina were stolen during a national holiday from a museum in the Sicilian port city of Messina.

Two days earlier, Italian police said they had recovered three paintings by the French masters Paul Cézanne, Pierre-Auguste Renoir and Henri Matisse that were taken this year from a private museum near the northern city of Parma.

A report by Europol this month found that robberies at European museums are becoming increasingly violent, with thieves sometimes brandishing guns, assaulting staff and using sledgehammers, axes and even explosives to smash their way to targeted loot.

world.title: What could Meta’s US settlement mean around the world – and what now for other claims against firm?
world.snippet: Other governments could seek similar concessions, while separate legal action is pending in places ranging from Kenya to the Netherlands ...
world.content:
In October 2021, Abrham Meareg’s father, a professor of chemistry in Ethiopia’s northern town of Bahir Dar, was shot at close range and died outside his family home. This was in the middle of the country’s civil war.

For weeks, Facebook’s algorithm had actively promoted posts calling for the academic to be murdered, according to Meareg and Foxglove, a nonprofit organisation supporting Meareg’s lawsuit against the company in Kenya. These posts included photos of his father and his home address.

Meareg filed the lawsuit in 2022. He said he repeatedly asked Facebook to remove the posts and the company did nothing. Nearly four years later, the case has still not been heard. Foxglove said Meta, Facebook’s parent company, had “fought tooth and nail to avoid responsibility”.

Meareg said: “It’s a matter of numbers to them, a matter of statistics. It has been proven multiple times that our lives do not matter to them.”

On Wednesday, Meta settled a lawsuit brought by 29 US states who argued it had designed addictive products that hooked young people. The social media company agreed to pay $18bn and to change certain features of its platform in the US. California’s attorney general said it was a victory that would make “a world of difference for children and their families”.

But elsewhere in the world, in jurisdictions as far flung as Amsterdam and Nairobi, other claims have yet to be heard. Far bigger questions about the power of a single US technology company to shape politics and democracy everywhere on Earth are still to be answered.

For the US, the settlement is a victory. A jury has done what the US Congress could not – put controls on a powerful tech company. As a part of the settlement, Meta has said it will set time limits on children’s use of its platforms Facebook and Instagram and block night-time usage.

For Meta, the settlement is also a victory. Its share price rose in the hours after the deal was announced. Its CEO, Mark Zuckerberg, was not forced to testify. The sum it is to pay, while not meaningless, is far less than the states had sought – $200bn – or the amount Meta itself had suggested in a court filing it might have to pay, which was up to $1.4tn.

For the rest of the world, however, the picture is more mixed. The limits Meta will put on its US platform are, in large part, similar to limits the UK and Australia have already achieved through regulation. There are certain concessions Meta has now made that other governments could also demand: for example, while the UK plans to ban under-16s from social media platforms, it may wish to ask Meta to impose a default daily use limit of two hours for under-18s, which is what the company has agreed to in the US.

None of this meaningfully changes the equation for Meareg or what his case represents, which is that a massive US company, unaccountable to voters, unbound by transparency requirements, owns a worldwide digital commons that shapes reality for billions of people.

Whether courts and governments outside the US have the power to confront this fact is a far thornier question.

The central issue of Meareg’s case is Meta’s algorithm. This is the system that decides what content to show users of Facebook and Instagram. It sees you linger over a video about knitting sweaters, for example, and then decides you’ll like one about how to care for your spider plant.

It sees teenage girls watch diet content and shows them anorexia influencers. It sees young men search for bodybuilding content and shows them Andrew Tate. It is alleged to have amplified content that promoted the ethnic cleansing of the Rohingya in Myanmar. It contributed to the election victory of Donald Trump.

Meareg’s lawsuit rests on the claim that this algorithm promoted the posts that called for the death of his father, and that Facebook’s sparse moderation in east Africa did almost nothing to prevent this.

In the early days of the Meta trial in the US, it seemed plausible that states would push the social media firm to finally make some changes to this algorithm. Those changes had the potential to fundamentally alter how the company does business. Meta’s algorithm is intended to keep users scrolling, stuck on the platform, and then it shows them ads.

But that is not what appears to have happened. The terms of the settlement will slightly change what is shown to minors, in that they will not necessarily have personalised feeds. But it is hard to see this concession changing the equation in war zones or creaking democracies.

Arturo Béjar, an ex-Facebook employee and whistleblower, said the limitations were “the equivalent of saying: ‘Well, you can smoke as many cigarettes as you can in two hours a day.’ It doesn’t make the cigarettes any safer.”

It may be up to groups and individuals elsewhere in the world to try to push for these larger changes. It will be an uphill struggle.

In Kenya, the high court recently ruled that Meareg’s case against Meta could go ahead, after years of legal manoeuvring from the company to try to prevent it. It could now be heard in the next year.

Rosa Curling, Foxglove’s co-executive director, said: “Meta’s lawyers have spent years trying to prevent this important case being heard, thankfully without success. We hope that the news from the US is a sign that Mark Zuckerberg’s time is finally up.”

In the Netherlands, Repro Uncensored, a nonprofit organisation tracking digital censorship, hailed the US settlement as a “major victory”. Repro Uncensored has an ongoing legal case against Meta in the Netherlands for alleged discrimination against queer accounts, and plans further action in other European countries.

Martha Dimitratou, Repro Uncensored’s executive director, said: “The next stage of accountability must address not only addictive design but algorithms, discriminatory moderation and automated decision-making. These systems shape civic participation and democracy, and the companies controlling them must be held accountable globally.”

The European Commission released a charge sheet against Meta this summer saying the company’s features, including its infinite scroll, contributed to “unhealthy habits and compulsive use”.

That charge sheet is part of an investigation into Meta that the commission launched in 2024. It may lead to Europe pushing for larger changes from Meta, including to its personal algorithm.

It is unclear whether any of these groups or parties can succeed. Meta appears to fear US regulators and courts: after all, it caved after just four days of its US trial. It does not appear to be as intimidated by regulators elsewhere.

Earlier this year it managed to dodge a class-action lawsuit brought by a group of Rohingya refugees over its alleged role in contributing to a genocide in Myanmar. It will have the help of the Trump administration in opposing any EU regulation that could curb its reach in Europe.

Meta declined to respond to questions about either Meareg’s or Repro Uncensored’s cases. In an earlier response to whistleblower allegations that it fuelled violence in Ethiopia and Myanmar, it pushed back forcefully, saying it was “just not true” that the company put profits over safety. Regarding Meareg’s case, it has said it employs staff with local knowledge and expertise to “catch violating content” in Ethiopia.

Meareg said he believed that Meta expected him to give up. “They don’t know how I am determined for justice,” he said. “It is the thing you do for the person you love. If you love someone – and I loved my dad from my heart – then he needs justice. He needs a public apology. There has to be accountability.”
